title: ‘Water yes, mining no!’: the 87-year-old farmer who became a nature hero in Colombia
summary:
Porfirio Garcés is one of the ‘Jerico 11’, who face kidnapping charges after opposing a copper mine. Now, with a far-right president prioritising extraction, their fight has become more urgent

In the rural hamlet of Palo Cabildo in Colombia’s western Andes, 87-year-old farmer Porfirio Garcés tends to his anthuriums in the garden of his small house. He talks with passion about his vinyl record collection, which ranges from classical to pop music, but his main interest now lies elsewhere: his homeland, to which he feels a deep connection – and his desire to protect it.

Numerous water sources originate in the area, supplying not only Jericó, where Garcés lives, but also several neighbouring towns in the Antioquia region.

Photograph: Luis Bernardo Cano Southern frontlines: Latin America and the Caribbean Colombia ‘Water yes, mining no!’: the 87-year-old farmer who became a nature hero in Colombia Porfirio Garcés is one of the ‘Jerico 11’, who face kidnapping charges after opposing a copper mine. Now, with a far-right president prioritising extraction, their fight has become more urgent Supported by About this content Luis Bernardo Cano in Bogotá Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n the rural hamlet of Palo Cabildo in Colombia ’s western Andes, 87-year-old farmer Porfirio Garcés tends to his anthuriums in the garden of his small house. He talks with passion about his vinyl record collection, which ranges from classical to pop music, but his main interest now lies elsewhere: his homeland, to which he feels a deep connection – and his desire to protect it. Numerous water sources originate in the area, supplying not only Jericó, where Garcés lives, but also several neighbouring towns in the Antioquia region. A sign with a clear message hangs on the main porch of his property: “Yes to water.” “We don’t want to wake to the roar of machinery drilling into and destroying our land, destroying the poetry of the landscape,” says Garcés. “We must defend our water sources. Without water, we will die of thirst.” View image in fullscreen The countryside around the farming village of La Soledad in Jericó, which is affected by the proposed mine. Photograph: Luis Bernardo Cano Since last year, Garcés and 10 other local farmers have faced formal charges for opposing the Quebradona copper mining project, promoted by the multinational AngloGold Ashanti through its subsidiary Minera de Cobre Quebradona . He has since become a symbol of the resistance movement against Quebradona in Jericó. Social protests in support of the “Jericó 11” gained strength in August as the nature defenders awaited new court hearings. “Water yes, mining no! Water yes, mining no!” the crowd chanted before the hearings, which postponed sentence until March 2027. The charges against the 11 farmers are “simple” kidnapping (the moving of someone against their will, without factors such as ransom or serious bodily harm), aggravated theft and assault. Although the judge at the initial hearings on 13 May 2025 rejected the prosecutors’ request to keep the 11 farmers under house arrest, they are still awaiting trial. View image in fullscreen People protest in Jericó to oppose the Quebradona mining project and support the 11 farmers. Photograph: Luis Bernardo Cano AngloGold Ashanti arrived in the region 15 years ago to extract copper in an area traditionally known for agriculture, where crops such as coffee, plantains, cassava, beans and corn are cultivated. Its first exploration licence was granted in 2007, covering nearly 8,000 hectares (about 19,800 acres). This initial stage was extended for 11 years – the maximum permitted by Colombia’s mining code – after which the company consolidated the properties to apply for an exploitation licence to start extraction. However, in 2019, the National Environmental Licensing Authority archived the application due to lack of technical information, requiring the company to conduct new studies before it could begin mining. In August, Colombia’s National Mining Agency approved an extension of the exploration phase at Quebradona until 8 December 2027. Mining has not yet begun, as the company still needs to address social and environmental concerns and complete additional studies, but Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s far-right president since August, has aggressively prioritised expanding oil, gas and mineral extraction, including fracking, as a core part of his economic platform.
